So the margin rises by about 0.31 for each 1.0 of price, roughly 0.31×(price − 3.2), and does not match price minus the stated cost of 1.0. plans:
This round, hold at 5.51 to see whether Firm B stays near 6.19. That separates the effect of Firm B's move from my own and avoids starting a war just after Firm B raised its price. Next round:

insights: Judge prices by the profit actually reported. It behaves like profit ≈ 0.31×(price − 3.2)×units, so the effective cost is about 3.2, not 1.0. My units ≈ K − 29.5×(my price) + 20×(Firm B's price), with K + 20×(Firm B) ≈ 219.5 when Firm B is at 6.19 and ≈ 208 when it is at 5.63. The one-round best price is about (K + 20×Firm B)/59 + 1.6. That gives about 5.32 with Firm B at 6.19 and about 5.13 with Firm B at 5.63, but profit is flat near the top, so moving ±0.2 costs little. Firm B's price is the main driver: its jump to 6.19 raised my profit by about 8.4, far more than any change in my own price. Keeping Firm B high matters more than fine-tuning, so avoid sharp cuts that might provoke it. Pricing above Firm B costs a lot (27.6–30 profit in the 5.8–6.0 rounds when Firm B was at 5.64). Firm B is usually sticky but sometimes makes jumps.

The Round 204 result shows that $1.98 can scale to 31+ units when competitive pressure eases. The $0.98 margin per unit at $1.98 is the true efficiency frontier—tested across 70+ rounds, no other price point has demonstrated comparable profit sustainability. The competitor's price jump to $1.93 created a $0.25 price gap that the market exploited through volume expansion, not margin compression. This is a regime shift: we've moved from a low-margin-high-volume defensive market to a high-margin-high-volume growth market.

insights: Firm B's jump to 7.92 signals a structural shift away from the 7.31-7.38 equilibrium that held for rounds 104-200.
